title: SonarQube, SonarQube for IDE and quality gates
summary: Use local analysis and CI quality gates, and interpret coverage without treating it as behavior proof.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Master SonarQube, SonarLint, and SonarCloud: Ultimate Guide to Enhancing Your Code Quality

richText: Static analysis reads source code without running the application. It can find risky patterns, duplicated code and maintainability problems.
SonarQube for IDE, formerly SonarLint, reports issues while editing. Connected mode can align its rules with the project on SonarQube.
SonarQube Server stores analysis results on a server you operate. SonarQube Cloud, formerly SonarCloud, provides hosted project analysis.
A scanner analyzes the chosen project revision and sends results to the server or cloud service. The Maven scanner integrates this step with a Java build.
Use IDE feedback for a quick local fix. Use CI analysis for a shared result tied to the revision under review.
A quality gate checks configured conditions on analysis results. It may include issues, duplication or coverage for new code.
A passing gate means those configured conditions passed. It does not prove that every API behavior, permission rule or deployment works.
Coverage measures which code ran while tests executed. Sonar imports a report produced by a coverage tool such as JaCoCo; Sonar does not run the tests itself.
High coverage can coexist with weak assertions. An effective check verifies meaningful outcomes such as an unauthorized record remaining inaccessible.
Make CI wait for the gate result when release policy depends on it. A scanner upload completing is not automatically a passing gate.
Analyze the same revision that the build and review use. Keep the project key, source paths and coverage-report path explicit in CI configuration.
Provide the analysis token through a CI secret. Do not place the token in pom.xml, the command history or a public log.
Review each finding in its actual context. Fix a real issue; record a justified suppression when a rule does not apply.
Keep generated code out of human-code analysis when the project policy allows it. Do not exclude difficult application code only to improve a score.
